Read the light before you land.

At the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth hangs low. MoonNav traces both against the real terrain — LOLA laser altimetry with lunar curvature, NAIF SPICE ephemerides checked against JPL Horizons — and turns it into sunlight intervals, direct-to-Earth windows and comparisons you can defend.

Three things decide whether a polar site works
Sunlight

The Sun never climbs more than about 1.5° above the pole's horizon geometry, so a ridge tens of kilometres away can switch a site between light and shadow.

Earth in view

Earth hangs low and nearly fixed in the lunar sky, wobbling a few degrees with libration. Whether it clears local terrain decides direct-to-Earth line of sight.

Terrain and date

Crater walls, massifs and lunar curvature shape every horizon, and the Sun's path shifts through the month and the seasons. Small moves change the answer.

Glossary
Lunar latitude / longitude
Planetocentric latitude (angle from the equatorial plane at the Moon's centre) and east-positive longitude from 0° to 360°.
Body-fixed frame
Axes attached to the rotating Moon. MoonNav uses MOON_ME, the mean-Earth/polar-axis frame that LOLA products use.
Azimuth
Compass direction of a target measured clockwise from local north: 0° N, 90° E, 180° S, 270° W.
Elevation
Angle of a target above the local horizontal plane. Negative means below it.
Horizon (terrain)
For each azimuth, the highest elevation angle of the surrounding terrain as seen from the site, including the drop caused by the Moon's curvature.
DEM
Digital elevation model: a grid of terrain heights. MoonNav uses LOLA LDEM_75S_240M, 240 m per pixel.
LOLA
Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter; it measured the Moon's topography with laser pulses.
Ephemeris
Tabulated positions of bodies over time. MoonNav uses the JPL DE440 ephemeris through SPICE.
Libration
Small apparent wobbles of the Moon as seen from Earth (and of Earth as seen from the Moon), which move Earth by several degrees in the lunar sky.
Local ENU
East-North-Up coordinates at the site, used to turn 3D vectors into azimuth and elevation.
Direct sunlight
Some (or all, depending on the rule) of the Sun's disk is above the terrain horizon.
Solar irradiance
Sunlight power per square metre arriving at the Moon, about 1361 W/m² at 1 AU, varying with the Sun's distance.
DTE (geometric)
Direct-to-Earth line of sight: Earth is above the terrain (and the antenna mask).
RF link
Actual radio communication performance. It needs power, antennas, frequencies and ground stations — MoonNav does not compute it.
Uncertainty
How much a result could differ because of data resolution, coverage and modelling choices. MoonNav reports quality reasons instead of a made-up confidence percentage.

Scientific methods and limitations

Method version moonnav-method-1.0.0. How MoonNav turns ephemerides and terrain into visibility states, intervals and optional energy estimates. Full equations and validation evidence are in docs/SCIENTIFIC_METHODS.md in the repository.

1. Coordinates, frames and time

Sites use planetocentric latitude (north positive) and east-positive longitude in [0°, 360°). West-positive input is converted explicitly. The body-fixed frame is MOON_ME, which the NAIF kernel moon_de440_250416.tf defines as MOON_ME_DE440_ME421 — aligned with the DE421 mean-Earth/polar-axis frame that the LOLA gridded products use, so terrain and ephemeris share one frame.

Heights are radii relative to a 1737.4 km sphere (the LOLA reference). The observer sits on the bilinearly interpolated LOLA surface plus a configurable height (default 2 m).

Times are entered and reported in UTC. Internally SPICE converts UTC to TDB with the naif0012.tls leap-second kernel; timestamps without a Z are rejected.

2. Sun and Earth geometry

For each timestamp, spkcpo returns the vector from the fixed surface site to the Sun or Earth in MOON_ME, with light-time and stellar-aberration correction (LT+S, apparent geometry). Lunar orientation, including physical libration, comes from the binary PCK moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc; positions from de440s.bsp. No fixed-obliquity shortcut is used.

The vector is rotated into local East-North-Up: horizontal = √(E² + N²), azimuth = atan2(E, N) mod 360, elevation = atan2(U, horizontal). At exactly 90°S, “north” follows the site’s longitude meridian.

Validation: for three sites (pole, Mons Mouton, a rim point) and 15 epochs each, MoonNav’s Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation agree with independent JPL Horizons observer tables to better than 0.01° (automated test).

3. Terrain and horizon

The DEM is LOLA LDEM_75S_240M (PDS, product version 2.0): a 3812 × 3812 polar stereographic grid, 16-bit heights × 0.5 m, 240 m pixels. The reader validates the PDS3 label keywords, file size and SHA-256 before use. Locations outside 75°S–90°S are no-data — never zero.

The horizon is traced along great circles in 0.5° azimuth bins out to 300 km, sampling every 240 m. Each sample is placed at its true 3D position (reference radius + LOLA height), so lunar curvature is included; the horizon at an azimuth is the maximum elevation angle along the ray. Rays that leave coverage are flagged “truncated” and carry an upper bound computed for hypothetical terrain 11 km high (above any lunar topography) beyond the edge.

4. Visibility states and intervals

The Sun (radius 695,700 km) and Earth (equatorial radius from pck00011.tpc) are treated as disks. With centre elevation e, apparent radius r and horizon h: visible if e − r ≥ h; partial if the disk straddles h; terrain-blocked if e + r ≤ h with e + r > 0; below horizon if e + r ≤ min(h, 0); unknown when the decision would change if unseen terrain beyond coverage reached its bound.

The rule that counts as “lit” is explicit: any part of the disk (default), full disk, or centre point. The visible fraction of a partly hidden disk uses the circular-segment area above a locally straight horizon line.

The interval is sampled at the chosen step; every state change is then refined by bisection to the chosen tolerance (default 10 s). Sensitivity tests at 60 min, 15 min and 5 min steps agree within one minute once refined.

pages.mainText:
About MoonNav

A decision-support tool for comparing lunar south-pole sites and dates by terrain-aware sunlight and geometric Earth visibility.

MoonNav answers a planner's first questions about a polar site: when does sunlight reach it, when is Earth in line of sight, and how do those answers change with a few kilometres of position or a few days of schedule. It computes Sun and Earth directions with NASA/JPL's SPICE toolkit and compares them with a 300 km terrain horizon traced through NASA's LOLA elevation model, including the Moon's curvature.

Results are reproducible: every scenario is immutable, and every analysis records the terrain product, kernel set, method version and their checksums. Values carry labels that say whether they are source data, calculated, modelled or precomputed — and unknown is reported as unknown.

MoonNav began as a response to the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge “Lunar Landing Site Navigator”. It is an independent research and education prototype: not NASA-owned, endorsed or flight-certified, and it does not select approved landing sites.

buttons.text: Rendering diagnostics (FPS, frame time, long tasks)

pages.mainText:
Known limitations

What the current build cannot claim. These limits are also printed in every exported report.

Terrain resolution

The analysis DEM is LOLA LDEM_75S_240M (240 m pixels). Near-field terrain within about a kilometre is smoothed, so small rocks, boulders and local slopes are not represented. Results are not a landing-hazard assessment.

Coverage

Terrain covers 75°S to the pole. Horizon rays that reach the coverage edge are flagged; if unseen terrain could change a decision, the state is reported as unknown.

Named sites

Featured sites are IAU feature centres from the USGS Gazetteer. They are not NASA candidate landing regions or approved sites.

Power

Energy is an idealized estimate from user-supplied panel assumptions. Thermal effects, dust, storage, MPPT and wiring losses beyond the derating factor are not modelled.

Communication

Direct-to-Earth results are geometric line of sight only. No RF link budget, antenna pattern, pointing or ground-network availability is modelled.

Imagery

No optical imagery (Moon Trek/LROC) is integrated; maps are derived from LOLA elevation.

Ephemeris horizon

Analyses are limited to the DE440s kernel span (about 1849–2150) and to 400 days and 20,000 samples per analysis.

Earth disk

Earth is treated as a sphere with its equatorial radius; its oblateness and atmosphere are ignored.

Prototype status

MoonNav is an independent research/education prototype for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It is not NASA-owned, endorsed or flight-certified.

Privacy

What MoonNav stores and why.

Account data. Your name, email address, a salted password hash (scrypt), session records (with IP address and browser user agent, for security), your role and display preferences. Passwords are never stored in plain text.

Workspace data. Projects, scenarios, analysis results and reports you create. Scenarios and results are immutable so they stay reproducible.

Security records. Audit events for sign-in-related administration, role changes, data approvals and report sharing. These are append-only.

Cookies. One HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie. No advertising or analytics cookies are set.

Your controls. Settings → Profile lets you export your data as JSON and delete your account. Deletion removes your workspaces, sessions and credentials and anonymises your user record; public scientific source provenance is kept.

Public pages. Coordinate lookups on the public explorer are rate-limited by IP address; the address is not stored with the result.

Results are calculated from public NASA/JPL data products under stated assumptions and limitations. MoonNav provides them “as is”, without warranty. Always check the methodology, data sources and known limitations.
